input.idea:
What if creating short-form videos took only 2 minutes?

A promotional concept introducing TikMaker as an AI-powered tool that transforms simple ideas into ready-to-publish vertical videos. The video highlights the time-consuming process of traditional content creation, including brainstorming, scriptwriting, finding visuals, editing and animating. It then introduces TikMaker, demonstrating how the platform automates these steps and generates a complete motion graphics video from a single idea. The goal is to attract content creators, faceless creators and social media marketers while testing whether they would be interested in using such a tool.

template.reason: Your idea already follows a problem-then-fix shape. It opens on the slow manual process (brainstorming, scripting, finding visuals, editing, animating), then shows TikMaker turning one idea into a finished video on screen. The template runs a little shorter than 45 s, so keep the pain part tight and give the demo most of the time.

hooks.text: What if making a short video took only two minutes?
Brainstorm, script, find visuals, edit, animate... all for one short video?
Everyone making short videos without AI is just wasting their time.

hook.text: What if making a short video took only two minutes?

research.facts:
- A short-form vertical video is usually shot or built in a 9:16 frame. It is the only shape that fills a phone screen with no black bars above or below.
- Since October 15, 2024, YouTube counts any new vertical or square upload up to 3 minutes long as a Short. Landscape (16:9) videos stay regular videos, even when they are short.
- YouTube CEO Neal Mohan said in June 2025 that Shorts were averaging more than 200 billion views a day. A 2024 figure reported in the coverage was 70 billion.
- Making a video by hand takes real time. A survey by the video app Rizzle put the average at about 7 hours for 1 to 5 minutes of video, with answers ranging from 2 to 300 hours. That covers videos in general, not only Shorts.
- AI is now common in video work. Wyzowl's 2026 survey, as reported by other sites, found 63% of video marketers have used AI tools to make or edit videos, up from 51% a year earlier.
- Video is widely used for marketing: Wyzowl reports that 91% of businesses use video marketing in 2026, tied for its all-time high.

sources.title: YouTube Shorts Now Averages 200 Billion Daily Views (TheWrap)
Tubefilter: YouTube Shorts 200 billion daily views
How Long Does It Take To Create A YouTube Video? (Rizzle)

scenes.voiceover: What if making a short video took only two minutes?
scenes.visual: Big stopwatch counting from 0:00 to 2:00, next to a phone showing an animated 9:16 explainer video with a labeled diagram

scenes.voiceover: Say you want to explain a tech topic in a short video. No face, just clear visuals.
scenes.onScreen: Explain a tech topic. No face.
scenes.visual: Empty phone frame in 9:16 with a blinking question mark and a small 'faceless' icon; tech icons (code brackets, chip, cloud) float around it

scenes.voiceover: But explaining it well is the hard part. You need a script that teaches step by step, and visuals that show each step.
scenes.onScreen: Script that teaches + visuals for every step
scenes.visual: Split screen: on the left a messy document with crossed-out lines, on the right empty boxes waiting for diagrams

scenes.voiceover: And motion graphics mean animating every arrow, label and diagram by hand.
scenes.onScreen: Every arrow. Every label. By hand.
scenes.visual: Animation timeline crowded with keyframes, a cursor dragging one arrow at a time into a diagram

scenes.voiceover: That's what TikMaker is for. It turns one idea into an educational motion graphics video.
scenes.visual: The crowded timeline collapses into the TikMaker app icon, which slides into the center of the phone frame

scenes.voiceover: First, you type your idea. Just one sentence.
scenes.visual: TikMaker input field, a one-line tech idea typed in and the generate button clicked

scenes.voiceover: Second, TikMaker writes the script scene by scene, with the voiceover and the words shown on screen.
scenes.visual: TikMaker screen where the scene list appears: hook, problem, explanation, each with voiceover and on-screen text

scenes.voiceover: Third, it animates every scene as motion graphics in a nine by sixteen frame that fills the whole phone screen.
scenes.visual: TikMaker preview player playing the animated scenes, diagrams and labels moving in, in a full vertical 9:16 frame

scenes.voiceover: So you focus on what you want to teach, and TikMaker turns it into a vertical video ready to post.
scenes.visual: The finished explainer video playing full screen on a phone, then a check mark next to 'Ready to post'

prompt.system:
You are the producer of a short-video channel (TikTok, Reels, Shorts).
Your job in this step: choose how the video will be told, by picking ONE template
from the list you are given. You do not write the video yet.

You get the channel, the video idea and the templates.
Pick the template whose "when to use" fits the idea best; the length matters less.
A template's "needs" are the facts its required scenes are built on. Pick one the idea
can fill with its OWN facts: a rise-to-success story needs a success to show, a how-to
needs steps, a list needs items. If the idea lacks what a template needs, that template
does not fit, however close its topic is.
Never invent a template: answer only with an id from the list.
score: 5 = made for this idea and the idea has every fact it needs, 3 = workable,
1 = nothing in the list fits.
reason: one or two sentences for the creator, in plain English, about this idea.
prompt.user:
Channel: TikMaker and AI coding. Mostly TikMaker itself: what it can do, how a video gets made with it, new features and how it is being built with AI (build in public). Around that, short concrete videos about other AI tools, vibe coding and Claude Code: one problem or one feature per video, shown on screen rather than told.
Audience: Creators who want to make short videos faster with AI, and developers or beginners who build apps with AI and want to work faster without breaking things.

Idea: What if creating short-form videos took only 2 minutes?

The video highlights the time-consuming process of traditional content creation, including brainstorming, scriptwriting, finding visuals, editing and animating. It then introduces TikMaker, demonstrating how the platform automates these steps and generates a complete motion graphics video from a single idea. The goal is to attract content creators, faceless creators and social media marketers while testing whether they would be interested in using such a tool.
Wanted length: about 45 s
Face on camera: no, a faceless video

Templates:
- id: analogy-explainer
  name: Explained with characters
  what: A concept explained through a small invented world or everyday analogy
  when to use: An idea that is an abstract concept (economics, health, finance) that becomes clear as a story.
  needs: problem, step, concept-term, real-case, lesson
  length: 26–63 s
- id: app-list
  name: Free apps list
  what: A quick list of apps, one per scene, each shown on screen
  when to use: An idea that recommends several apps or tools for one device or audience.
  needs: app-count, device-or-audience, app-name, app-feature
  length: 14–62 s
- id: brand-origin
  name: Rise of a brand
  what: From a humble start, through hardship, to a big brand
  when to use: An idea that is the history of a brand, product or founder that has already grown big: the idea gives the success to show (users, money, years). Not a creator telling why they built their own tool.
  needs: year-or-result, brand, founder, start, hardship, time-jump, result-number
  length: 43–80 s
- id: build-it-fast
  name: Build it fast
  what: Show the finished thing, then every step that built it
  when to use: An idea where the viewer can build something real in minutes with a tool.
  needs: result, time, tool-name, step, screen-recording
  length: 20–51 s
- id: dark-true-story
  name: Creepy true story
  what: A dark or strange true story told step by step to a shocking ending
  when to use: An idea that is a real crime, legend or eerie event.
  needs: place-or-person, event, ending
  length: 15–51 s
- id: explained-in-time
  name: Explained in 60 seconds
  what: A complex topic explained in a promised short time, often to an unlikely audience
  when to use: An idea that is a complex topic the viewer finds hard and wants explained quickly.
  needs: nothing special
  length: 35–54 s
- id: how-to-steps
  name: How-to steps
  what: A how-to promise followed by numbered steps on screen
  when to use: An idea that is a concrete task the viewer wants to do with a tool, in a few steps.
  needs: task, tool-name
  length: 32–43 s
- id: myth-vs-reality
  name: Myth vs reality
  what: What people think, then how it really works, with the proof
  when to use: An idea that corrects a common belief or reveals a hidden side of something familiar.
  needs: belief, background, reality, step, twist
  length: 26–59 s
- id: new-tool-news
  name: New tool news
  what: A just-released free tool, its benefits, a quick demo and a comment-keyword offer
  when to use: An idea that is news about a newly released or newly free tool.
  needs: who-released, tool-name, benefit, keyword, resource
  length: 30–107 s
- id: pain-to-fix
  name: Problem then fix
  what: The broken or painful way first, then the tool that fixes it, shown working
  when to use: An idea where a tool fixes a pain the audience recognises, including a creator telling why they built their own tool: the pain they had, then the tool that fixes it.
  needs: pain, task, screen-recording
  length: 30–40 s
- id: plot-recap
  name: Story recap
  what: A plot, journey or character backstory retold event by event
  when to use: An idea that recaps an episode, myth, game lore or a character's story.
  needs: story-name, setting, ending
  length: 48–181 s
- id: product-promo
  name: Product promo
  what: A product's benefits shown one by one through its interface, ending on where to get it
  when to use: An idea that promotes one product or service.
  needs: product-name
  length: 11–30 s
- id: question-answered
  name: Big question answered
  what: A why or how question, answered step by step with diagrams
  when to use: An idea that is a question the audience has wondered about.
  needs: question
  length: 43–71 s
- id: ranked-countdown
  name: Top N countdown
  what: Ranked items counted down to number one
  when to use: An idea that ranks a set of things by some measure.
  needs: rank-count, ranked-thing, rank-number, item-name, item-detail
  length: 25–60 s
- id: rapid-facts
  name: Rapid-fire facts
  what: Many short facts in a row, one per scene, with the strongest kept for last
  when to use: An idea that is a collection of short surprising facts around one theme.
  needs: theme, fact
  length: 40–56 s
- id: single-fact
  name: One surprising fact
  what: One fact built up line by line to a short reveal
  when to use: An idea that is a single surprising or eerie fact that fits in under 20 seconds.
  needs: topic
  length: 7–16 s
- id: software-tutorial
  name: Software how-to
  what: A finished result first, then the steps to make it in the software
  when to use: An idea that is a specific thing to make in a common program (PowerPoint, GitHub, a no-code tool).
  needs: result, software
  length: 14–53 s
- id: tool-deep-dive
  name: Tool explained
  what: What a tool is, how it differs, and what it really does
  when to use: An idea that explains one popular tool or model and how to think about it.
  needs: tool-name, difference, main-point
  length: 49–78 s
- id: tool-spotlight
  name: Tool spotlight
  what: One website or tool shown working, often as a numbered series part
  when to use: An idea that is a single useful website, repo or tool the viewer probably has not seen.
  needs: tool-category, series-part, screen-recording
  length: 10–56 s
- id: tool-tips-keyword
  name: Tool tips list
  what: Numbered tips for one tool, each named and then shown working, ending with a comment-keyword offer
  when to use: An idea that is a handful of concrete tips, skills or add-ons for one tool the audience already uses.
  needs: tool-name, tip-count, tip-number, tip-name, keyword, resource
  length: 47–88 s

prompt.system:
You write the opening line (hook) of a short vertical video (TikTok, Reels, Shorts):
the words shown and spoken in the first two seconds, which decide whether people keep watching.

Write THREE different hooks for the idea.
The formulas show openings that have worked: follow one where it fits this idea (fill it
in, do not copy its example) or write your own. formulaId = the formula's id, or null for
a hook of your own.
Fill a formula only with what the idea says: never claim something it does not
(no "I switched from…", no number, no result the idea does not give).
Each hook: one line, at most 12 words, plain spoken English, no hashtags, no emojis.
score: 5 = people stop scrolling, 3 = fine, 1 = weak.

  type: story
  formula: "[The most dramatic line spoken in the story]"
  example: Why did you kill my wife and daughter ?
- id: i-switched-from
  type: story

  example: I switched from Cursor to Claude Code.
- id: everyone-without-is-wasting

  formula: Everyone using [tool] without [feature] is just wasting their [resource].
  example: Everyone using Claude without skills is just wasting their tokens.
- id: you-are-the-only
  type: contrarian
  formula: You are the only [statement that sounds impossible].
  example: You are the only person alive.
- id: you-might-think
  type: contrarian
  formula: When you [everyday action], you might think [misconception]...
  example: When you visit a website, you might think that your computer is connecting with

prompt.system:
You write the script of a short vertical video (TikTok, Reels, Shorts).

Tell ONE connected story. The idea may be written as loose thoughts in any order: sort
them into the order the template's scenes tell (the problem before the fix, the cause
before the result), and let every scene follow from the one before it – the voiceovers
read in a row must make sense as one spoken text. A scene that promises something ("what I learned", "here's why") is
followed by the scene that says it.

The template is a guide: a structure that has worked for videos like this – its scenes,
their order and how they link. Follow it where it serves this idea; change the order,
leave a scene out or add one when that tells this story better. A "repeatable" scene
may appear several times in a row (one per step or item). Put every template scene you
leave out in "skipped" with a short reason.
A scene's "facts" come from the idea and the facts found online only – never invent a
tool, a number or a result.
When the idea has no fact for a scene, leave it out if it is optional; if it is required,
fill it with what the idea does say rather than with an invented claim.
Its "creative" parts are yours to word.

The first scene is the hook: say the chosen hook as it is, and show its key words.
The template's links ("→ next") and the transition phrases are examples of how scenes
can follow each other; use them only where they read naturally. End the way that fits
this video best: the CTA formulas show endings that have worked – use one, or write
your own, or none if no ending asks for one.
The call to action never sends people to a link, a website, a download or a giveaway
the idea does not mention – then pick a CTA formula that needs none of those.

For every scene:
- voiceover: what is said, natural spoken English
- onScreen: the key words shown big, not the whole sentence
- visual: what the viewer sees, concrete (a terminal running a command, a settings page,
  an app icon), never "something engaging"
- needsRecording: your call – true when the scene is shown best with the creator's own
  screen recording rather than a picture the video editor draws.

Keep within the limits. Each scene lasts about as long as its voiceover: fill the wanted
length – add more steps or items with the repeatable scenes, keep the optional scenes
that help – rather than stopping short.

Template: Problem then fix – The broken or painful way first, then the tool that fixes it, shown working
Scenes:
- opening / hook (2–2.8 s): Shows or states the wrong way people do it. [required] → next: contrast; facts: pain; creative: who
- build / setup (2.4–4 s): Sets the scene of the task. [required] → next: sequence; facts: task
- build / problem (3–7 s): Names what goes wrong. [optional] [repeatable] → next: open-loop-payoff; facts: problem
- core / reveal (2.2–4.6 s): Names the fix. [optional] [repeatable] → next: sequence; facts: tool-name
- core / demo (3–7 s): Shows the fix working on screen. [required] [repeatable] → next: sequence; facts: screen-recording
- climax / benefit (3.4–6.6 s): States what changed. [optional] → next: bridge; facts: gain
- close / cta (3–3 s): Points to the full guide. [optional] → next: none; facts: resource

Transition phrases:
- sequence: First, | Second, | Third, | First is | Second is | Third is
- contrast: But | Instead | Instead of just | But instead, | but in reality, | but that's not how
- bridge: So if you want | So just | To get the full | For a PDF | So want to try it for yourself? | Now you might be wondering...
- open-loop-payoff: It's called | You have probably heard of | Here's the easiest way | All roads lead to Rome... | And that's why... | Anthropic just dropped

CTA formulas (types allowed: none):
- none: end on the last scene, without a call to action (skip the cta scene)

Limits, from the analysis of successful videos:
- speak at most 3.4 words per second
- a scene lasts at most 9 s, the hook at most 5 s
- at most 15 words on screen in a scene

prompt.system:
You are the motion designer of a short vertical motion video (1080x1920, 30 fps).
The script and the pictures (blocks) are decided; your only job is how everything moves,
so the whole video reads as one flow instead of a row of separate slides.

For every scene pick the transition into it. For every block, in order, pick:
- entrance and enterFrames: how it arrives on its word
- exit and exitFrames: how it leaves when the next block takes its place (or the scene ends)
- drift (optional): slow motion while it holds the screen
- moves (optional): on a later word of the voiceover it moves to y (% of the frame's
  height, its centre) at scale – a deliberate change of place or size, not a nudge
- carry (optional, only the scene's last block): it stays into the next scene and glides
  to that scene's first place instead of leaving; the next transition is then "cut"
And in "idea", say in a sentence or two what your motion is: the main direction, which
move marks which kind of moment.

Each block already animates its own content inside itself (list items, nodes, numbers
counting); you decide how the block as a whole arrives, moves and leaves.
Use the principles below as knowledge of what works and why – the choices are yours.
Answer with one entry per scene and one per block, in the same order as given.
prompt.user:
Principles:
- At any moment one thing moves and holds the eye; everything else is still or settles. Why: The viewer can follow only one moving thing. Several pictures animating at once in the same place read as a pile, not as a sequence – nothing is understood and the frame looks unstable. In this video: Never let two blocks enter or travel in the same place at the same time. When a new block arrives, the old one has already left or is leaving the opposite way.
- Every move says something: arriving, leaving, growing in importance, turning into something else, moving on. Why: Motion without a reason is decoration; decoration on every element is noise. When each move matches what the voice says at that moment, the motion explains instead of distracting. In this video: Pick an entrance for what the block MEANS at that word: a number that is the payoff can pop or zoomSettle; a next item in a list slides in from the same side as the previous one; a calm explanation can just fade.
- Keep one direction of travel for things that are 'the next one' – a list, steps, the story moving on. Why: A consistent direction builds a mental map: new things come from the right, old ones leave to the left, so 'forward' always looks the same. A different direction on every cut reads as random. In this video: Choose a main direction for the video (e.g. in from the right, out to the left) and use it for every 'next' moment. Change direction only to mark a real change: a contrast, a turn in the story, a new chapter.
- Carry something across a cut: the same object, the same position, the same shape or the same direction of movement. Why: A cut where nothing connects resets the viewer's attention to zero. A match – one element staying, or the motion of the outgoing scene continuing into the incoming one – makes two scenes feel like one flow. In this video: When the same logo or object is in two consecutive scenes, carry it (link) instead of letting it leave and come back. When nothing is shared, let the outgoing block leave in the same direction the incoming one arrives from, so the motion continues.
- Carry at most one element across a cut. Why: One carried element guides the eye to the next scene; several moving at once cross paths and the eye loses which one to follow. In this video: One link per cut. Everything else leaves.
- Arrivals slow down into place; departures speed up and leave. Why: Real objects accelerate and decelerate. Something that arrives fast and settles feels confident; something that leaves accelerating feels gone. Linear motion looks mechanical. In this video: The code already eases every entrance out and every exit in. Use keyframe moves for deliberate travel, not for small nudges.
- Leaving is quicker than arriving. Why: The viewer cares about what is coming, not about what is going. A long exit holds attention on something that no longer matters. In this video: Exits about 6–8 frames, entrances about 8–12 frames at 30 fps. Longer only for a deliberate, dramatic reveal.
- Bigger changes take longer; small ones are quick. Why: A move across the whole frame in a few frames is a jump; a tiny fade over a second is sluggish. Duration should match how far and how much something changes. In this video: A full-frame transition or a long keyframe travel: 12–18 frames. A badge or a small element appearing: 6–10 frames.
- A small overshoot and settle gives an element weight – use it for the few moments that matter. Why: Overshoot draws attention because it is a little surprising. On every element it stops being a surprise and the video feels bouncy and cheap. In this video: pop, bounceIn and zoomSettle* are the overshooting presets – reserve them for the hook, the key number and the verdict. Most blocks should arrive calmly (fade, slide, scaleIn).
- Prepare the viewer just before the payoff. Why: A brief build-up – a pause, a small zoom in, the previous element clearing the stage – makes the reveal land harder than if it simply appears. In this video: Before the key moment, let the stage clear (the previous block leaves early) or give the incoming block a slower, larger entrance than the rest.
- When several things belong together, they arrive one after another in reading order, not all at once. Why: A staggered arrival shows the order to read them in; everything at once is a wall the viewer has to sort out themselves. In this video: List items, schema nodes and logos already stagger inside their block. Do not add a second stagger on top of it.
- Text and numbers must stop moving long enough to be read. Why: The eye cannot read moving text. Continuous drift is fine for a picture, not for a sentence or a number the viewer has to take in. In this video: Ken Burns (zoomIn, float…) suits objects and screenshots held longer than about 2 s, not code, terminals, lists or numbers.
- Vary the motion between beats, but from a small set used consistently. Why: The same fade on every element for a minute is boring; twenty different effects look like a template demo. Two or three entrances with a clear role each read as a style. In this video: Give each kind of moment its own move (next item, contrast, payoff, calm explanation) and keep that pairing through the whole video.
- A frame with no picture is a pause – the cut into it should feel like the stage clearing. Why: A statement scene works because it is empty. If the previous picture lingers or is pushed out noisily, the pause is lost. In this video: Before a statement scene, let the last block leave cleanly (fade or a short exit) by the end of its scene.

Entrances:
- fade: appears softly in place
- slideUp: travels in from below, moving up
- slideDown: travels in from above, moving down
- slideLeft: travels in from the right, moving left
- slideRight: travels in from the left, moving right
- scaleIn: grows in from slightly smaller
- pop: pops in with a small bounce
- zoomSettleRight: flies in from the right, overshoots its size, settles – strong
- zoomSettleLeft: flies in from the left, overshoots its size, settles – strong
- zoomSettleTop: flies in from above, overshoots its size, settles – strong
- zoomSettleBottom: flies in from below, overshoots its size, settles – strong
- zoomIn: comes in from bigger, shrinking into place
- blurIn: comes into focus from a blur
- spinIn: spins in
- flipIn: flips in around its vertical axis (3D)
- bounceIn: bounces in
- dropIn: falls in from above the frame
- rollIn: rolls in from the left

Exits:
- none: no exit – cut away on its last frame
- fade: fades out in place
- slideUp: speeds away upwards, out of the frame
- slideDown: speeds away downwards, out of the frame
- slideLeft: speeds away to the left, out of the frame
- slideRight: speeds away to the right, out of the frame
- scaleOut: shrinks a little as it fades
- burstOut: punches up in size and turns as it fades – strong
- zoomOut: grows past the viewer as it fades
- blurOut: blurs away
- spinOut: spins away, shrinking
- flipOut: flips away around its vertical axis (3D)
- dropOut: falls out of the bottom of the frame
- rollOut: rolls away to the right

Drifts:
- zoomIn: slowly grows
- zoomOut: slowly shrinks
- panLeft: slowly moves left
- panRight: slowly moves right
- panUp: slowly moves up
- panDown: slowly moves down
- float: drifts and tilts gently around its place
- rotateCW: turns slowly clockwise
- rotateCCW: turns slowly anticlockwise

Transitions into a scene:
- cut: a hard cut – the next scene is simply there
- slideLeft: the next scene pushes in from the right, moving left
- slideRight: the next scene pushes in from the left, moving right
- slideUp: the next scene pushes in from below, moving up
- slideDown: the next scene pushes in from above, moving down
